title: Get started
text: Immutable documents · Rust · Python · browser Keep the documents. Rebuild the view. CouchDB-inspired map/reduce over an immutable document log. A Rust engine keeps the facts durable; every index and live view is a replaceable cache. Write the computation in AssemblyScript and run the same WebAssembly in Python or a browser worker. Try it in your browser ↗ Build a portable view 01 Append Immutable JSON documents → 02 Map Emit a key and contribution → 03 Fold Derive a rebuildable live view Foldlite DB 0.4.1. Python 3.11+ is required. Native wheels are provided for Linux x86-64 and ARM64, macOS Intel and Apple Silicon, and Windows x86-64. Upgrading an existing database? Follow the step-by-step upgrade guide , and check the consolidated changelog for release history and compatibility changes. Install python -m pip install foldlitedb==0.4.1 Installing a matching native wheel needs neither Rust nor Node. To build from a checkout instead, install Rust/Cargo 1.90+ and a platform C compiler and linker, then run from the repository root: python -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install . python examples/portable_metrics.py On Windows, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate in an MSVC build environment. Node is needed only to author or rebuild views. To build a wheel, run python -m pip wheel . --no-deps --wheel-dir dist , then install the resulting .whl on a matching platform. Installing a built wheel needs neither Rust nor Node. See the release guide for PyPI Trusted Publisher setup and publication. A native metric in a few lines The bundled metrics module maintains count, sum, minimum, maximum, and mean by metric. Start with a fresh metrics.fold log: from foldlitedb import Database, View metrics = View.bundled("metrics") with Database("metrics.fold", metrics) as db: documents = db.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result == { "count": 2, "sum": 12, "min": 4, "max": 8, "mean": 6, } Rust runs both map and reduce in a bounded Wasm interpreter. An accepted batch is appended and synced to the document log. A derived checkpoint lives separately in metrics.fold.cache ; one active database owns the log through metrics.fold.lock . Database and View are the primary names; PortableDatabase and PortableView are aliases. Append freely. Name when useful. Each unnamed add(payload) creates a new observation. Supply a source-scoped ID when identical retries should count once. Documents are immutable; conflicting reuse raises DocumentConflict . with Database("metrics.fold", metrics) as db: saved = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}, id="measurement-3") assert db.add(saved.payload, id="measurement-3") == saved documents += (saved,) External sources can supply their own IDs and monotonically increasing positions. To represent an update, append another observation and let an ordered view fold its meaning. Read once, follow changes rows() follows bounded snapshot pages. query() also returns a cursor for later changes: with Database("metrics.fold", metrics) as db: snapshot = db.query() db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 1}) updates = db.changes(since=snapshot.cursor) assert updates.rows[0].result["mean"] == 4 db.checkpoint() Validation, mapping, and reduction finish before a batch is committed. A view error leaves the current batch uncommitted. Checkpoints are optional accelerators, written on request or clean close. For a multi-metric consumer, collect every snapshot and change page. The persistent consumer example also replaces its application state from a fresh snapshot when a cursor expires. A cache can always be reconstructed Keep the document log and exact view module; the cache can be discarded. Reopening verifies the complete log, reuses a valid checkpoint, and executes Wasm only for its uncached suffix. Missing or incompatible checkpoints rebuild from the original batches. Opening with a different module rebuilds its derived view from the same documents. with Database("metrics.fold", metrics) as db: expected = [(r.key, r.state, r.result) for r in db.rows()] db.rebuild() assert [(r.key, r.state, r.result) for r in db.rows()] == expected Rebuild starts a new cursor generation. Its cost is a linear log read plus map/reduce work for uncached batches; no unmeasured throughput is promised. Current indexes and view history grow in host memory. Back up the log: a disposable cache does not make the only source copy disposable. The same module, entirely in a browser Open the static playground , import JSON or JSONL, and watch groups update locally. A dedicated worker executes the same compiled module as Python; JavaScript owns browser grouping and in-memory storage. Export resolved documents before reloading or closing. The browser example includes resource copying and a complete static page. Browser persistence, log/history compaction, and multiple native views per database remain future work. Keep exploring Run the telemetry collector for 2,500 readings, safe source retries, and cache-loss recovery, or the catalogue example for an ordered item lifecycle. Use preview(payload) to inspect a view's map output when a document produces no rows. Write a portable view ↗ A complete AssemblyScript module, custom build, and browser integration. The native Python API ↗ Appends, snapshots, changes, checkpoint, and rebuild. Documents and caches ↗ Identity, deterministic folds, durability, and cache validation.

text: The same view. A new place to run it. Your browser. Your live database. CouchDB-inspired map/reduce, running right here. An AssemblyScript view maps your documents and reduces each group in WebAssembly. No server required. Local workspace Starting WebAssembly worker… 0 retained documents 0 live groups 0 committed sequence Ready replay verification 01 Bring your documents Drop a JSON or JSONL file A document array, or one document per line. Choose a file ↗ Up to 1,024 small documents per import. Files stay in this browser. Add a measurement Metric Value Add + Paste JSON or JSONL Raw documents Import documents 02 Watch your views update metrics@1 map → group → reduce Start live stream Live metrics computed by the WebAssembly view Metric Count Mean Min Max Loading the example… Observed range min — ● — max · dot = mean ↻ Rebuild & verify Export documents ↓ Reset example Loading the shared view module. ✓ AssemblyScript → WebAssembly → dedicated worker Inspect the module View Loading… SHA-256, verified before execution Loading… Storage In memory. Export documents before reloading this page. Isolation No host imports. Maximum 16 MiB of WebAssembly memory. Worker requests have a deadline. JavaScript retains documents and groups emitted keys. The AssemblyScript module performs every map and reduction. This is the same compiled artifact used by the native engine. Enable JavaScript to run this local map/reduce example. Write a view once. Run it here or in Python. The metrics module accepts documents with a string metric and a finite numeric value . Its map emits the metric as a key. Its reducer maintains count, sum, minimum, and maximum; finalization computes the mean. Other document shapes are ignored by the map. Numbers use double precision in both environments. Keep large identifiers as strings. Strings must be valid Unicode; each module request is limited to 256 KiB of encoded JSON. Browser · no backend import { BrowserDatabase } from "./portable/client.js"; const db = await BrowserDatabase.connect(); await db.add({ metric: "latency_ms", value: 42 }); const rows = await db.rows(); console.log(rows[0].result); db.close(); Python · the same metrics.wasm from foldlitedb import Database, View view = View.bundled("metrics") with Database("metrics.fold", view) as db: db.add({"metric": "latency_ms", "value": 42}) row = list(db.rows())[0] print(row.result) Your documents are the source of truth Try the live stream, add a few measurements, then select Rebuild & verify . A fresh in-memory database replays every retained document through the same module and compares its complete view states and results. Existing views keep their cursors. Exported JSON includes document identities, sources, positions, and payloads. Importing it again is an identical replay: each retained document counts once. Changing an existing identity or position fails the whole batch. Use those same records to rebuild the native database. A portable computation preview. This browser database keeps documents and view history in memory. Export them to keep your work. The live stream is simulated locally; this page makes no requests containing your documents. Python provides the persistent Rust document-log engine with a disposable view cache.

title: Portable views
text:
CouchDB-inspired views, from Python to the browser Write a view once. Run it in either environment. A portable view contains both its map and its reducer. AssemblyScript compiles them into one WebAssembly module, executed by the Rust engine or a browser worker. Try the browser playground Write a custom view Foldlite DB 0.4.1. Install with python -m pip install foldlitedb==0.4.1 . Each native document log has one derived view; the browser host keeps its documents and view in memory. A native database from Python Build prerequisites are Python 3.11+, Rust/Cargo 1.90+, and a platform C compiler and linker. From the repository root: python -m pip install . python examples/portable_metrics.py The Rust engine and precompiled view modules are included. Node is needed only for authoring or rebuilding AssemblyScript. To produce a wheel locally, run python -m pip wheel . --no-deps --wheel-dir dist . Installing the resulting wheel on a matching platform needs no compiler. See environment setup for virtual-environment and Windows notes. Start the following example with fresh database files: from foldlitedb import Database, View view = View.bundled("metrics") with Database("metrics.fold", view) as db: documents = db.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result["mean"] == 6 snapshot = db.query() db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}) assert db.changes(since=snapshot.cursor).rows[0].result["mean"] == 5 retained = tuple(db.documents()) Rust owns the append-only document log, immutable identity, derived checkpoints, group states, snapshots, and changes. Its bounded Wasm interpreter executes both mapping and reduction. The log is independent of the module; a checkpoint is a disposable cache. rows() follows paginated snapshots; explicit query() and changes() support resumable reads. The Python reference covers every portable method. Two bundled views Metrics accepts payloads with a string metric and finite numeric value . Valid documents emit one number under their metric key; malformed shapes, missing fields, nulls, and nonnumeric values emit nothing. States contain {count,sum,min,max} ; finalized results add mean . Empty states use null minimum, maximum, and mean. This view supports merge. Invalid contributions, states, and numeric overflow fail. Catalogue accepts {category:string,id:string,title:string,deleted?:boolean} . Each category folds item IDs to their latest titles. An event with {category,id,deleted:true} removes that item. Finalization returns {count,items:{id:title}} . Event order matters, so this view does not support merge. Malformed documents emit nothing; item IDs are limited to 65,535 UTF-16 code units. Author a complete view Use a Node.js runtime matching ^22.23.4 || ^24.22.1 || >=26.12.1 and install the pinned SDK dependencies from the repository root: npm ci --prefix views For a custom module, save this complete source as views/assembly/examples/metric-totals.ts . It groups numeric values by metric and returns a running total. The SDK handles UTF-8 buffers, finite JSON, allocation, dispatch, and error envelopes. import { JSON, View, Emission, object, numeric, number, dispatch } from "../sdk"; export { abi_version, input_ptr, input_capacity, output_ptr } from "../sdk"; class MetricTotals extends View { constructor() { super("metric-totals", false, "1", "1"); } map(document: JSON.Value): Emission[] { const doc = object(document); if (doc == null) return []; const metric = doc.get("metric"); const value = doc.get("value"); if (metric == null || metric.type != JSON.Types.String || !numeric(value)) { return []; } return [new Emission(metric, value!)]; } identity(): JSON.Value { return JSON.Value.from(0); } add(state: JSON.Value, values: JSON.Arr): JSON.Value { if (!numeric(state)) return this.fail("Invalid total state"); let total = number(state); for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) { const value = values.at(i); if (!numeric(value)) return this.fail("Expected a numeric contribution"); total += number(value); } if (!isFinite(total)) return this.fail("Total overflowed"); return JSON.Value.from(total); } finalize(state: JSON.Value): JSON.Value { if (!numeric(state)) return this.fail("Invalid total state"); return state; } } const view = new MetricTotals(); export function execute(length: i32): i32 { return dispatch(view, length); } From the repository root, compile the source and generate its digest manifest with one command: npm run build:view --prefix views -- assembly/examples/metric-totals.ts --out-dir .build Both path arguments are relative to views/ , regardless of the caller's working directory; absolute paths also work. The output directory is created if needed. The source filename determines the outputs: views/.build/metric-totals.wasm and views/.build/metric-totals.json . Use letters, digits, underscores, dots, or hyphens in the source filename. The manifest records the compiled descriptor and SHA-256; its descriptor name may differ from the filename. Browser connect({name}) uses the artifact filename stem. The command applies the same pinned compiler settings as the bundled build and ignores ambient JSON_* settings. It validates the ABI and descriptor before replacing successful outputs; compilation or validation errors leave existing artifacts intact. Choose a separate output directory such as .build ; SDK, dependency, script, and bundled asset directories are protected. The ordinary npm run build --prefix views still builds only the two bundled examples. From the repository root, load the same bytes from Python: import json from pathlib import Path from foldlitedb import Database, View manifest = json.loads(Path("views/.build/metric-totals.json").read_text()) custom = View("views/.build/metric-totals.wasm", sha256=manifest["sha256"]) with Database(":memory:", custom) as db: db.add_many([{"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result == 12 The map receives payloads only, not host IDs or positions. Include domain metadata inside the payload if your computation needs it. Keys, states, and contributions can be structured JSON. State is passed explicitly to every update; requests must not depend on mutable module globals, clocks, randomness, or undeclared external data. Hosts instantiate the module afresh for operations. add must preserve contribution order and produce equivalent state when an input sequence is split into successive batches. Implement merge and set mergeable=true only when compatible independent states can be combined correctly. The example leaves merge disabled. Bump the view version for changed behavior and the state version for incompatible formats; rebuild the module and manifest together. A new compiler can also change the module digest. Use the module on a static website The playground imports JSON arrays or JSONL, appends measurements, streams simulated updates, exports resolved records, and verifies replay. All document processing stays in its worker. The same module bytes power the Python example; JavaScript owns browser grouping and storage. The Rust document-log engine is not part of the browser build. To create your own page, copy the installed package's browser files and bundled modules. Run this Python from the repository root: from pathlib import Path from foldlitedb import portable_assets target = Path("browser-demo/portable") target.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) for resource in portable_assets().iterdir(): if resource.is_file(): (target / resource.name).write_bytes(resource.read_bytes()) Save this as browser-demo/index.html . Browser methods are asynchronous; addMany returns a batch-result object, while Python's add_many returns a tuple of documents. Foldlite DB in the browser 
Loading…
python -m http.server 8000 --directory browser-demo Open http://localhost:8000 ; opening the file directly is insufficient for module workers and fetch. Production deployments can serve these files over HTTPS. Copy the entire resource directory, including client.js , worker.js , host.js , and errors.js , so their module imports resolve. For the custom totals view, copy views/.build/metric-totals.wasm and metric-totals.json into browser-demo/portable/ , then change the connection to: const db = await BrowserDatabase.connect({ name: 'metric-totals', base: new URL('./portable/', import.meta.url), }); The browser verifies the manifest's SHA-256 and descriptor before execution. db.info contains initial stats. Compare (await db.stats()).module_sha256 with Python's View.sha256 to confirm the exact artifact. Every method below returns a Promise. A resolved document is {id,payload,position,source,sequence} ; a batch result is {documents,inserted,replayed,sequence,cursor} . inserted and replayed are counts, and documents contains the resolved input records in order. db.add(payload, {id?, source?, position?} = {}) → resolved document db.addMany(payloads, {source?} = {}) → batch result db.ingest(records) → batch result db.preview(payload) → [{key,value}, ...] db.export() → resolved document[] db.stats() → {documents,sequence,cursor,module_sha256,descriptor, checkpoints,storage:"memory",memory_bytes} db.replay() → {equivalent,documents,groups,module_sha256} add accepts an optional identity; unnamed appends create new observations. addMany commits one bounded batch. ingest retains supplied IDs, sources, and positions; identical re-imports count as replays. Exported sequence fields describe progress in the current worker and are regenerated on import. Preserve id , payload , position , and source ; compare keys, states, and results across databases rather than sequence fields or cursors. preview maps one payload without appending documents, advancing progress, or running the reducer. Use it to diagnose an empty view: await db.preview({metric:'loss',value:4}) returns [{key:'loss',value:4}] , while an incompatible payload may return [] . Python exposes the same diagnostic as db.preview(payload) . A successful preview checks mapping only; an actual append can still fail reduction or host limits. query({limit,cursor,after,key,start_key,end_key,prefix,inclusive_start,inclusive_end}) returns {rows,cursor,after,complete} ; continue with both returned cursor and after and preserve the selector and inclusive flags. Each row contains {key,state,result,sequence} . rows(options) collects all snapshot pages into an array and accepts the same selectors. Choose exact key , either/both range bounds, or a string/array prefix ; combining modes fails. Bounds are inclusive by default, and explicit null is a bound rather than omission. Traversal is ascending. Queries use the same numeric and compound-key ordering and prefix semantics as Python. These queries select existing per-key results without combining them into another reduction. const page = await db.query({start_key: "temperature.c", end_key: "voltage", inclusive_end: false}); const temperatures = await db.rows({prefix: "temperature.", limit: 100}); // For a custom view emitting ["sales", customer, day] keys: const alice = await db.rows({prefix: ["sales", "alice"]}); Query continuation tokens bind the selector and snapshot; changing filters or reusing a 0.2.x query token fails explicitly. Page size can change. changes(cursor,{limit}) returns {rows,cursor,complete} ; continue with its returned cursor until complete. replay() uses the original committed batches to compare keys, states, and results, reporting the boolean equivalent without changing current cursors. Browser failures reject with DatabaseError or its subclasses DocumentConflict , SourceOrderError , and CursorExpired , exported from client.js . Each has a stable code and name matching its class name, plus a descriptive message . Use a class or code instead of parsing message text: import { DocumentConflict } from './portable/client.js'; try { await db.add({metric: 'loss', value: 4}, {id: 'observation-1'}); } catch (error) { if (error instanceof DocumentConflict) { console.error(error.code, error.message); } else { throw error; } } Source names beginning with _ are reserved for metadata. They are retained, exported and replayed, and advance source progress, but do not contribute to views in either host. The computation contract and limits Operation Input Output descriptor Module request Name, view version, state version, ABI, merge capability map A batch of document payloads An emission array per document, including zero emissions identity Empty request Initial JSON state for a group add State and ordered contributions Updated JSON state finalize State Public JSON result merge Two compatible states Combined state, when supported Payload nesting is measured from each payload root, independently of transport wrappers, with a 64-level limit. ABI response depth retains its separate 64-level envelope limit. The v1 ABI uses UTF-8 JSON with a 256 KiB request limit and a separate 256 KiB response limit, both including envelopes. Modules have no host imports and at most 16 MiB of linear memory. The native host imposes a fuel budget. The browser client runs a dedicated worker with a 15-second default deadline, configurable through timeoutMs from 1 through 60,000 milliseconds. Expiry terminates the worker and loses its in-memory state. Both hosts limit an ingestion batch to 1024 documents and 4096 emissions, and snapshot pages to 1024 entries. Encoded map and per-group add requests can reach the ABI byte limit earlier. The browser additionally caps retained documents at 20,000 and 16 MiB of encoded records, distinct groups at 4096, and history at 100,000 entries and 32 MiB of encoded rows. Its public request envelope is capped at 4 MiB. These are component limits, not a bound on the whole browser process. A failing batch does not commit a prefix. Portable JSON numbers use IEEE-754 double precision, as in JavaScript. Python and the native engine reject integer inputs that cannot be represented exactly as doubles; use strings for exact large identifiers. A view's response may spell a large double the way JSON.stringify does, but an inexact integer, such as one from 64-bit integer arithmetic, is rejected. Positions and cursor sequences are nonnegative JavaScript-safe integers. Floating-point sums preserve ordered inputs; arbitrary merge trees can change rounding. See numerical reproducibility . Retain documents; regenerate views Keep the document log and exact compiled module. A persistent metrics.fold log has separate metrics.fold.cache and metrics.fold.lock siblings. One active owner holds the log. Accepted immutable batches are synced before acknowledgement; clean close or checkpoint() writes an atomic derived snapshot. Reopen verifies the complete log, reuses a matching cache prefix, and executes Wasm for only the uncached suffix. Missing, corrupt, or different-module caches rebuild from the original batches. To change computation, open the same log with the new module; documents remain unchanged. A human version label cannot override a changed digest. Keep the previous module if its previous result must remain reproducible. rebuild() explicitly recomputes the current view, checkpoints it, and starts a new cursor generation. Reconstruction is a linear log read plus map/reduce work for uncached batches; current indexes and history grow in host memory. Cache acceleration avoids computation, rather than the full validation read, and has no unmeasured throughput guarantee. with Database("metrics.fold", view) as live: expected = [(row.key, row.state, row.result) for row in live.rows()] live.rebuild() assert [(row.key, row.state, row.result) for row in live.rows()] == expected To copy resolved documents into a separate log, preserve their original order: with Database("copy.fold", view) as rebuilt: rebuilt.ingest(retained) assert list(rebuilt.rows())[0].result["mean"] == 5 For larger streams, iterate db.ingest_many(records, batch_size=100) ; each yielded result commits one bounded batch. db.documents(limit=100) exports resolved records at a pinned snapshot. Browser exports include an additional engine sequence field; Python accepts them after constructing Document objects: import json from pathlib import Path from foldlitedb import Document, Database, View view = View.bundled("metrics") records = json.loads(Path("exported-documents.json").read_text(), parse_int=float) documents = [Document(r["id"], r["payload"], int(r["position"]), r["source"]) for r in records] with Database("from-browser.fold", view) as db: for result in db.ingest_many(documents): print(result.inserted, result.replayed) The final snippet expects an exported JSON array from the metrics view. Browser payload numbers use IEEE-754 doubles; parse_int=float preserves those semantics even when a large double is serialized without a decimal point. Safe source positions are converted back to Python integers when constructing documents. Preserve input order; preserve batch boundaries too if exact engine sequence values matter. Compare computation outputs rather than database-local cursors. A new database or rebuilt cache receives a new generation, so obtain new cursors even when results match. A valid checkpoint preserves cursors across an ordinary reopen. Native documents persist in the log; a cache can always be reconstructed. Back up the log or an authoritative external stream: deleting the only source copy loses data. Browser state is in memory and is discarded on reload or close() . Export before closing and ingest those records into a new worker to restore it. Persistent browser storage, log/history compaction, and multiple native views per database remain future extensions. See the document and cache model .

title: Python API
text: Reference · development API The Python API Database uses one Rust engine for document acceptance, source order, durable commits, and replay. View identifies a portable Wasm computation or a versioned Python callback projection. View and packaged assets View(module, *, sha256=None) View.bundled(name="metrics") → View portable_assets() → importlib.resources Traversable Import these names from foldlitedb . module accepts Wasm bytes or a filesystem path. A View stores immutable module bytes and their sha256 ; an optional digest must match. Modules range from 1 byte through 16 MiB. The native database validates exports, imports, ABI, and descriptor when opening. bundled accepts "metrics" or "catalogue" and verifies the manifest digest. Metrics returns {count,sum,min,max,mean} ; catalogue returns {count,items} . See accepted payloads . portable_assets() exposes modules, manifests, and browser hosts; copy files with each resource's read_bytes() method. PortableView is an exact alias of View . It does not select another engine. Versioned Python callback views View(name, *, version="1", map=..., reducer=..., references=None) OrderedFold(initial, step, *, version, finalize=None) RustReducer(name, *, runtime=None, positioned=False) db.register(view) → view version Callbacks receive resolved Document objects, including the host-assigned ID and source position. A map yields ordered (key, contribution) pairs. The reducer provides identity , add , and finalize ; OrderedFold applies a Python step in accepted ingestion order. A callback batch can emit at most 4096 contributions. Keys, contributions, state, and results must be finite portable JSON. Callback code runs as trusted Python, without Wasm's execution or memory isolation, and must be deterministic and free of database mutations. Every append API uses native acceptance and deduplication. Maps, reducers, and finalizers stage their complete batch before its source documents are durably committed. Conflicting input, a failing callback, or invalid output commits nothing. Identical retries do not map again. Python view operations are synchronized, and returned JSON is copied. from foldlitedb import Database, Document, OrderedFold, View totals = View( "totals", version="1", map=lambda document: [("total", document.payload["value"])], reducer=OrderedFold(0, lambda state, value: state + value, version="1"), ) with Database("callbacks.fold", totals) as callback_db: callback_db.add({"value": 2}, id="first") observation = Document("second", {"value": 3}) assert callback_db.ingest([observation]).inserted == 1 assert callback_db.ingest([observation]).replayed == 1 assert next(callback_db.rows()).result == 5 with Database("callbacks.fold", totals) as callback_db: assert callback_db.query().rows[0].result == 5 callback_db.rebuild() assert callback_db.query("totals").rows[0].result == 5 Callback cache coverage and descriptors live in the disposable native checkpoint. Reopen restores matching groups and replays any uncached original batches. Missing caches and changed descriptors reconstruct from retained documents; rebuild() also recomputes registered callback views. Callback code and captured reference changes require a new view/reducer version or changed references . Retain the Python computation and its inputs when preserving reproducibility. Passing a callback view to Database makes it the primary query() / rows() view. Additional callbacks registered with register are queried by name. Snapshot pages use descriptor-bound cursors; historical pages reconstruct from the accepted batches and can cost a replay. Primary callback views explicitly reject changes() and preview() ; use a fresh query snapshot or call the mapper directly on a resolved document. Portable Wasm views retain their change feeds and preview operations. foldlitedb.projection.materialize_jsonl_view is an external-source accelerator: the external stream remains authoritative. It commits its consumed cursor and derived state together, binding both to the source generation and view/reducer/reference descriptor. A descriptor change rereads the external source instead of reusing its previous consumed watermark. Historical external projection snapshots are unavailable; obtain a fresh snapshot. This helper does not retain the external document history in its compact cache. Document: a named source observation Document(id, payload, position=None, source="default") Import Document from foldlitedb to construct records for ingest or ingest_many . Construction alone writes nothing. id is a stable, nonempty string naming one observation within its source ; payload is its finite JSON value. The same ID in another source names a different observation. Supply position when the upstream source already has ordered offsets. New positions must advance that source, with gaps allowed. If the source has stable IDs but no offsets, omit position : ingestion assigns one automatically. An identical named retry with position=None reuses the original position, even after newer records arrive. Input objects are not mutated; use documents() to export their assigned positions. Records returned by add , add_many , or documents always have resolved integer positions. The fields are id , payload , position , and source . Returned payloads are independent copies; changing a copy cannot update a stored document. Reusing an ID or position with conflicting content raises DocumentConflict . Append a new named observation to express a change. Source names beginning with _ are reserved for metadata. They are retained, exported and replayed, and advance source progress, but do not contribute to views in native or browser execution. Database Database(path, view=None, *, generation=None, reset=False) Database.migrate(source, destination) A Rust-native database executing one primary Wasm or Python callback view. view accepts a View , Wasm bytes, or a module path; omit it for bundled metrics. path accepts a filesystem path or ":memory:" . Parent directories must already exist. A persistent path is an append-only document log, with .cache and .lock siblings. Exactly one active owner may open it. Use a context manager or close() . Clean close checkpoints persistent derived state and releases ownership. Closing is idempotent; later operations raise DatabaseError . PortableDatabase is an exact alias. Reopen validates the complete log and reuses a compatible cache, then replays any uncached suffix. A missing or invalid cache rebuilds. Different module bytes automatically rebuild the view from the same documents. Reconstruction creates a new cursor generation; a valid checkpoint preserves generation across reopen. Old external-database files are not this log format. New databases use FOLDLOG2 frames with persisted predecessor hashes. Existing FOLDLOG1 logs remain readable and exportable but reject new appends. Close their owner, then call Database.migrate("old.fold", "new.fold") to verify and copy their original batches into a new log. The source is unchanged; an existing destination is never replaced. Verify the new log with the intended view before retiring the source backup. Stats report log.format and log.read_only . The upgrade guide walks through backup, source inspection, migration, verification, cutover, rollback, and application compatibility checks. Primary filenames ending in .cache or .lock , or containing .cache. , are reserved for sidecars. Conflicting source logs or symbolic links at auxiliary paths cause an error. Unrecognized cache bytes are preserved under a unique .cache.unrecognized.* filename when replaced by a valid checkpoint. reset=True is explicitly destructive. Native ownership locks remain held throughout reset; an active owner prevents it. Invalid modules are rejected before reset changes data. Reset I/O errors are reported and may leave an uncertain outcome. generation is an optional identity for an external source generation; a mismatch raises GenerationMismatch . from foldlitedb import Database, View with Database(":memory:", View.bundled("metrics")) as db: original = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, id="a") assert db.add(original.payload, id="a") == original snapshot = db.query() db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 8}) assert db.changes(since=snapshot.cursor).rows[0].result["mean"] == 6 retained = tuple(db.documents()) assert db.stats()["documents"] == 2 with Database(":memory:") as replay: assert replay.ingest(retained).inserted == 2 assert replay.ingest(retained).replayed == 2 Append and replay db.add(payload, *, id=None, source="default", position=None) → Document db.add_many(payloads, *, source="default") → tuple[Document, ...] db.ingest(documents) → IngestResult db.ingest_many(documents, *, batch_size=100) → iterator[IngestResult] add appends one finite JSON payload and returns its resolved Document(id, payload, position, source) . Omitted IDs are generated; omitted positions start at zero and advance per source. An identical named add or replay at an existing source position reuses the original document. Conflicting reuse fails; previously unseen positions must advance that source. IDs and sources are nonempty strings of at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes; positions range from zero through 2**53 - 1 . add_many eagerly consumes one iterable of payloads and commits atomically. Its returned records preserve input order. Every member is one payload, including an entire array; empty input returns () . Retrying unnamed payloads appends new observations. Documents are immutable; append a new observation to express a change. ingest takes Document instances with stable identities, payloads, and optional upstream positions. Its result contains inserted , replayed , and sequence . Identical replay performs no map work. ingest_many is lazy: you must iterate its results to write anything. Each yielded result commits a separate batch of 1–1024 records, defaulting to 100. A later error preserves earlier committed batches; the complete import is not one atomic transaction. An atomic batch has at most 1024 documents and 4096 emissions. The complete map request, including its envelope and newly inserted payloads, must fit 256 KiB; per-group add requests, states, and results must fit their own buffers. The log frame limit is 8 MiB. Reduce batch size for larger payloads. Validation, map, reducer, and limit errors leave the current batch uncommitted; successful persistent batches are synced before acknowledgement. Finite JSON uses IEEE-754 doubles and at most 64 nesting levels. Python and the native engine reject integer inputs not exactly representable as doubles, such as 2**53 + 1 , rather than rounding them; 2**53 + 2 is accepted. Accepted integers above 2**53 - 1 are returned as floats. Nonfinite values and invalid Unicode scalar strings fail. Use strings for arbitrary-precision identifiers. Retry-safe source batches If your telemetry export has offsets, retain them along with the source and stable reading IDs. Fully iterating the import below commits 25 batches; resending an old batch counts no readings twice: from foldlitedb import Database, Document source_records = [ {"id": f"gateway-07:{offset}", "offset": offset, "metric": "temperature.c", "value": 20 + (offset % 20) * 0.25} for offset in range(2500) ] records = [Document(r["id"], {"metric": r["metric"], "value": r["value"]}, position=r["offset"], source="gateway-07") for r in source_records] with Database(":memory:") as imported: results = list(imported.ingest_many(records, batch_size=100)) assert sum(result.inserted for result in results) == 2500 retry = imported.ingest(records[100:200]) assert retry.inserted == 0 and retry.replayed == 100 assert list(imported.rows())[0].result["count"] == 2500 If upstream provides IDs but no offsets, use named records with automatic positions instead. Do not invent new offsets from each export's row numbers: named = [ Document("probe-a:reading-1", {"metric": "temperature.c", "value": 20}, source="probe-a"), Document("probe-a:reading-2", {"metric": "temperature.c", "value": 21}, source="probe-a"), ] with Database(":memory:") as automatic: assert sum(r.inserted for r in automatic.ingest_many(named)) == 2 automatic.add({"metric": "temperature.c", "value": 22}, id="probe-a:reading-3", source="probe-a") assert automatic.ingest(named).replayed == 2 assert [record.position for record in automatic.documents()] == [0, 1, 2] For JSONL, construct each Document while iterating the file and pass that iterator to ingest_many . Keep source order, and retain resolved records when exporting. The complete telemetry example verifies summaries against a Python oracle, follows live changes, and reopens after deleting the cache. Inspect a payload's map output db.preview(payload) → list[{"key": JSON, "value": JSON}] preview runs only the current view's map function without appending a document or changing source progress, rows, or history. It does not run the reducer or guarantee that a later ingestion batch fits its limits. Use it to inspect unexpected zero-emission payloads: with Database(":memory:") as inspection: assert inspection.preview({"metric": "temperature.c", "value": 21}) == [ {"key": "temperature.c", "value": 21}, ] assert inspection.preview({"kind": "heartbeat"}) == [] assert inspection.stats()["documents"] == 0 Zero emissions are intentional filtering, not a rejection: ingestion still retains a valid document and advances its source progress. The bundled metrics view ignores shapes without a string metric and finite numeric value . Validate your application schema before ingestion if every retained document should contribute a reading. Rows, snapshots, and changes db.rows(view_name=<omitted>, *, view=None, key=<omitted>, start_key=<omitted>, end_key=<omitted>, prefix=<omitted>, inclusive_start=True, inclusive_end=True, limit=100) → iterator[Row] db.query(view_name=<omitted>, *, view=None, key=<omitted>, start_key=<omitted>, end_key=<omitted>, prefix=<omitted>, inclusive_start=True, inclusive_end=True, limit=100, cursor=None, after=None) → Snapshot db.changes(*, since, limit=100) → ChangePage rows lazily follows snapshot pages, pinning the committed prefix on first iteration. limit is a page size from 1 through 1024, not a total row limit. Omit view_name / view for the primary view or pass a registered callback view name; supply any JSON key , including null, via the key= keyword argument for exact filtering. No operation lock spans a yield into application code. A Row has key , reducer state , finalized result , and committed sequence . A Snapshot has rows , cursor , after , and complete . Continue with both returned cursor and after token, preserving every selector and inclusive flag. Page size may change. Changed selectors, another snapshot, and legacy query tokens fail explicitly. New ingestion does not change the pinned snapshot. with Database(":memory:") as db: db.add_many([ {"metric": "a", "value": 2}, {"metric": "b", "value": 8}, ]) page = db.query(limit=1) snapshot_cursor = page.cursor rows = list(page.rows) while not page.complete: page = db.query(limit=1, cursor=page.cursor, after=page.after) rows.extend(page.rows) assert [row.key for row in rows] == ["a", "b"] db.add({"metric": "a", "value": 4}) changes = db.changes(since=snapshot_cursor, limit=1) assert changes.rows[0].result["mean"] == 3 while not changes.complete: changes = db.changes(since=changes.cursor, limit=1) Range and prefix selection Use exactly one selector mode: an exact key , a range with either or both of start_key / end_key , or a prefix . Combining modes raises DatabaseError . Range bounds are inclusive by default; set inclusive_start=False or inclusive_end=False to exclude an endpoint. These options must be booleans. Omitted bounds are open; an explicit None is a JSON null bound. If the start sorts after the end, the result is empty. Traversal is ascending. A string prefix matches strings beginning with its characters. An array prefix matches arrays beginning with the same complete elements, compared by JSON structure rather than text. It includes an array equal to the prefix. Nested elements must match completely: ["sales", [2026]] does not prefix-match ["sales", [2026, 11]] . Empty string and array prefixes match all strings and arrays respectively. Other prefix types are invalid. All views, including named Python callbacks, use these selectors; for example db.query("sales", prefix=["alice"]) . Key order is null < false < true < numbers < strings < arrays < objects . Numbers compare numerically, so 2 precedes 10 . Strings compare by Unicode codepoint, independently of locale; this differs from CouchDB's ICU ordering. Arrays compare their elements recursively, then shorter arrays first when one is a complete prefix. Objects compare codepoint-sorted member names and each corresponding value recursively, then shorter equal member sequences first. Member insertion order does not affect equality or ordering. from foldlitedb import OrderedFold, View sales = View( "sales", version="1", map=lambda document: [( [document.payload["customer"], document.payload["day"]], document.payload["amount"], )], reducer=OrderedFold(0, lambda total, amount: total + amount, version="1"), ) with Database(":memory:", sales) as db: db.add_many([ {"customer": "alice", "day": "2026-11-01", "amount": 10}, {"customer": "alice", "day": "2026-11-02", "amount": 20}, {"customer": "bob", "day": "2026-11-02", "amount": 30}, ]) assert [row.result for row in db.rows(prefix=["alice"], limit=1)] == [10, 20] selected = db.query(start_key=["alice", "2026-11-01"], end_key=["alice", "2026-11-02"], inclusive_start=False) assert [(row.key, row.result) for row in selected.rows] == [ (["alice", "2026-11-02"], 20), ] Range queries select existing per-key state and results; they do not re-reduce the selected keys, return raw map emissions, or implement CouchDB group_level . Include the dimensions you need in emitted keys. The native host seeks a derived ordered index; browser and callback hosts sort their in-memory groups. The document log and ingestion sequence order are unchanged. changes returns committed group postimages after a snapshot or change cursor. since=0 reads retained history from the start. A page has rows , continuation cursor , and complete ; continue with that cursor. Repeated changes to a key in one batch coalesce. A page can split group updates from one batch. Zero-emission documents still advance progress. Cursors bind to the database generation and exact module. Checkpointed reopen can reuse them; rebuild, cache reconstruction, or module replacement expires them. A new database or browser worker cannot reuse another's cursor. There is no history compaction API. A persistent changes consumer that recovers Save a consumer's cursor together with the application state it describes. Change rows contain whole resulting group states, so replace each key's result. If the cursor expires, collect a fresh stable snapshot and replace the entire application state . Replaying from since=0 onto existing totals would double count. from pathlib import Path from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory from foldlitedb import CursorExpired def collect_snapshot(db): page = db.query(limit=1) state, cursor = {}, page.cursor while True: state.update((row.key, row.result) for row in page.rows) if page.complete: return state, cursor page = db.query(limit=1, cursor=page.cursor, after=page.after) def poll_changes(db, state, cursor): try: while True: page = db.changes(since=cursor, limit=1) state.update((row.key, row.result) for row in page.rows) cursor = page.cursor if page.complete: return state, cursor except CursorExpired: return collect_snapshot(db) # New dict replaces all old application state. with TemporaryDirectory() as directory: path = Path(directory) / "consumer.fold" with Database(path) as db: db.add_many([{"metric": "cpu.percent", "value": 20}, {"metric": "temperature.c", "value": 21}]) state, cursor = collect_snapshot(db) db.add({"metric": "temperature.c", "value": 23}) state, cursor = poll_changes(db, state, cursor) assert state["temperature.c"]["mean"] == 22 with Database(path) as db: # Clean close kept this cursor valid. assert db.changes(since=cursor).rows == () Path(str(path) + ".cache").unlink() with Database(path) as db: previous_state = state state, cursor = poll_changes(db, state, cursor) assert state is not previous_state assert state == {row.key: row.result for row in db.rows()} The runnable telemetry collector also persists its consumer checkpoint and proves that cache reconstruction preserves every resolved source record and summary. Checkpoint, rebuild, export, and inspect db.checkpoint() → dict db.rebuild() → dict db.get(id=None, *, position=None, source="default") → Document | None db.documents(*, limit=100) → iterator[Document] db.stats() → dict db.close() checkpoint atomically persists the current derived snapshot and returns stats plus checkpointed: true . Clean close also checkpoints. The cache is optional and is not rewritten after every append. Encoded snapshots are capped at 1 GiB. Checkpoint failures are reported, including during close; the synced source log remains intact and close releases ownership even on failure. rebuild replays original log batches through the current module, starts a new cursor generation, writes a checkpoint, and returns stats plus rebuilt: true . Documents remain unchanged. with Database("maintenance.fold") as db: db.add_many([{"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}]) expected = [(row.key, row.state, row.result) for row in db.rows()] assert db.checkpoint()["checkpointed"] is True assert db.rebuild()["rebuilt"] is True assert [(row.key, row.state, row.result) for row in db.rows()] == expected get resolves a single retained Document within source by either nonempty string id or safe integer position (returning None if absent, and raising DatabaseError when neither or both selectors are supplied). documents exports resolved records in original ingestion order at a snapshot pinned on first iteration. Page size is 1–1024. Back up these records or the log and retain exact view artifacts; the cache can be regenerated. Re-import through ingest or ingest_many . stats includes documents , groups , sequence , cursor , generation , module_sha256 , descriptor , and source checkpoints . storage is "append-only-log" or "memory" . The cache object reports status , bytes , and log_offset ; replay reports processed batches and documents ; log reports bytes , batches , recovered_tail_bytes , and writer_poisoned , which is true after an I/O error until the log is reopened. Engine sequence counts inserted documents and changed group states, rather than documents alone. Reopening always verifies the complete log, even with a valid cache. Current retained documents, indexes, and view history grow in host memory; there is no compaction or bounded total-memory guarantee. cache.status describes startup or the most recent checkpoint operation, not whether the in-memory view is usable. For example, status="missing" , bytes=0 , and replay.documents=2513 is healthy after rebuilding from a missing cache. The status stays "missing" until checkpoint() or clean close writes a cache. cache.bytes is the cache file size inspected or last written, not the memory used by the view; cache.log_offset is the reused or checkpointed log prefix. Status Meaning memory An in-memory database has no cache file. missing No cache was found on open; the log was replayed. invalid A cache could not be validated or did not match the log; the log was replayed. module-mismatch The cached view used different module bytes; the log was replayed through the current module. loaded A valid cached prefix was reused, with any remaining log suffix replayed. checkpointed A new persistent cache was written by checkpoint() or rebuild() . Errors and recovery DatabaseError extends ValueError . Validation and Wasm failures raise it; conflicting replay, source ordering, and invalid cursors use DocumentConflict , SourceOrderError , and CursorExpired where identified. A missing compiled extension raises an actionable RuntimeError . Opening an already-owned log fails. Complete log corruption fails rather than skipping records; only an incomplete final frame is recoverable as an interrupted append. A cache failure can be repaired by reconstruction. If an I/O error makes an append's acknowledgement uncertain, the writer is poisoned: later appends and checkpoints fail, reads still serve the last acknowledged state, and stats()["log"]["writer_poisoned"] is true . Close (which reports the failed checkpoint but releases the log), reopen, and retry using explicit resolved identities; an append that did reach the log becomes an identical replay. Keep backups of source data. Embedding the Rust engine Rust applications can depend on the foldlitedb-portable-engine crate directly. Engine::open(path, module_bytes) opens a log or ":memory:" , and Engine::execute takes the same JSON requests as the Python binding ( ingest , query , changes , documents , get , stats , checkpoint , rebuild , close ). The crate root exports its limits so callers can split work before submitting it: Constant Value Bounds ABI_BUFFER_BYTES 262,144 Each Wasm request and, separately, each response, including envelopes. A batch's one map request holds all newly inserted payloads; a per-group add request holds the previous state and that group's new values. MAX_BATCH_DOCUMENTS 1024 Documents in one atomic ingestion batch. MAX_BATCH_EMISSIONS 4096 Map contributions produced by one batch. MAX_LOG_FRAME_BYTES 8 MiB One encoded log frame (one committed batch). MAX_CACHE_BYTES 1 GiB One encoded derived checkpoint snapshot. MAX_JSON_DEPTH 64 Nesting of payloads, keys, states, and results. MAX_SAFE_INTEGER 2 53 − 1 Positions and sequences. Integers above it that a double represents exactly are accepted but read back as floats, so keep integer-typed domain values within it. Limit errors are host-neutral: they name the operation, the encoded size, and the limit, for example Wasm map request is 300123 bytes, which exceeds the 262144-byte ABI limit (ABI_BUFFER_BYTES) . Ingestion rejects any payload integer a double cannot represent exactly, naming the value, before mapping or writing. Engine::writer_poisoned() is a cheap, read-only health check that is true once an I/O error has made a durable append uncertain; Engine::is_writable() is true while the engine is open and not poisoned. To recover, execute close or drop the engine (both release the lock even if the final checkpoint fails), call Engine::open again, which verifies the log and discards an interrupted tail, and retry with explicit document ids or source positions.

title: Documents and caches
text: The model Documents and rebuildable caches Documents are immutable facts. A view is a deterministic fold over those facts. Persist the facts, verify cache dependencies, and make reconstruction an ordinary operation. Names are optional; documents are immutable add(payload) assigns an internal ID. Equal unnamed payloads are separate observations. A caller-supplied ID tells the host that an identical repeated call refers to one observation. An identical named retry skips mapping and keeps its original position, even after the source advances. Reusing that identity with different content is a conflict. Represent a lifecycle change by appending another document, then fold its meaning in an ordered view. The log never updates an accepted document in place. Positions track a source A position identifies a document's offset in its source. Automatic positions start at zero and follow that source's committed checkpoint. External logs can supply increasing offsets with gaps. from foldlitedb import Database, SourceOrderError with Database(":memory:") as db: first = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, source="training.log", position=10) db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, source="training.log", position=40) assert db.add(first.payload, source="training.log", position=10) == first assert db.stats()["checkpoints"]["training.log"] == 40 try: db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}, source="training.log", position=30) except SourceOrderError: pass else: raise AssertionError("New records cannot arrive behind the checkpoint") IDs and positions are scoped to a source. An existing position can identify a replay without a supplied ID; payload and any supplied ID must match. Previously unseen positions behind committed progress fail. Positions range from zero through 2**53 - 1 . Avoid mixing generated positions with external offsets unless they share a progression. For bulk input, use Document records with the upstream offsets you already have. When the source has stable IDs but no offsets, omit the position and let ingestion assign it; an identical named retry keeps its original assignment. See the retry-safe bulk import examples . ingest_many performs work only as you iterate its results, and each batch commits separately. Order belongs to the input Per-key reduction follows ingestion order, including document and emission order inside a batch. Source offsets do not sort documents across sources; timestamps do not reorder an existing fold. Applications choose domain order before ingestion and preserve it during replay. Maps receive payloads; the host owns identities, source positions, deduplication, and batches. Include needed domain metadata inside a payload. The bundled catalogue demonstrates a structured lifecycle fold whose answer can change if events are reordered. A map can intentionally emit nothing. Such a document is still retained and advances source progress; it simply contributes no view row. Use preview(payload) to inspect map output without storing a document, and validate application-specific reading schemas before ingestion when needed. Views must give equivalent state when the same ordered contribution sequence is split across successive add calls. Batch boundaries cannot define application semantics. Engine sequence values do depend on batches because they include document and changed-group records. The native log retains original accepted batches for exact internal reconstruction. The document log is durable A persistent Database("live.fold") owns three paths: the document log live.fold , a disposable checkpoint live.fold.cache , and an ownership lock live.fold.lock . One active owner may open the log. Close it before another process or instance opens it. ":memory:" creates no persistent files. An accepted batch is stored in a checksummed, hash-linked log frame and synced before acknowledgement. Validation, map, and reducer failures commit none of the current batch. ingest_many commits separate batches as iteration proceeds; earlier successful batches survive a later error. If an I/O failure interrupts acknowledgement, reopen and retry explicit identities to resolve whether a batch committed. Reopening validates the complete log. A partial final frame can be truncated as an interrupted write; complete corrupt frames fail explicitly. Recovery does not skip invalid committed documents. Preserve a backup of the log or an external authoritative document stream. Deleting the only source copy loses data. A checkpoint is a hint Document indexes, source checkpoints, reduced states, results, and history can all be derived again. checkpoint() atomically writes their current snapshot, and clean close also checkpoints. Encoded snapshots are capped at 1 GiB; checkpoint errors are reported even on close, while accepted log data remains intact. A failed close releases its native handle. The engine checks cache format, log identity, exact module digest, and the verified log-prefix offset and digest before reuse. With a valid snapshot, reopen loads its prefix and executes Wasm only for uncached suffix batches. Missing, corrupt, or incompatible cache data causes reconstruction from the document log. The log still must be read and verified linearly on every reopen; a checkpoint avoids computation, not that validation read. Checksums detect corruption, rather than authenticate files against someone who can rewrite them. After a successful reconstruction, stats()["cache"]["status"] can still be "missing" or "invalid" : it describes how startup handled the disk cache. The in-memory view is ready, and replay reports the work performed. A later checkpoint or clean close writes a new cache. Cache byte counts describe a disk file, not the view's memory use; the API reference lists each status . from foldlitedb import View view = View.bundled("metrics") with Database("live.fold", view) as live: live.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) expected = [(r.key, r.state, r.result) for r in live.rows()] retained = tuple(live.documents()) live.checkpoint() live.rebuild() assert [(r.key, r.state, r.result) for r in live.rows()] == expected with Database("copy.fold", view) as copied: copied.ingest(retained) assert [(r.key, r.state, r.result) for r in copied.rows()] == expected assert copied.ingest(retained).replayed == 2 rebuild() replays the existing log and writes a fresh checkpoint without changing its documents. It starts a new cursor generation. Export and re-import also preserve results when order is retained, but may use different batches and therefore different engine sequences. Preserve resolved records rather than payloads alone if identities and source progress must survive. Rebuild performs linear log I/O plus map/reduce work for uncached batches and emissions. Current indexes and history grow in host memory with the data; limits on one call are not a bound on total data. There are no measured rebuild-throughput guarantees or compaction API yet. A view revision is exact module bytes The module SHA-256 identifies mapping, reduction, state format, compiler, and SDK runtime. A matching human version label cannot override different bytes. Bump the view version for changed behavior and the state version for incompatible state schemas, then rebuild the module and manifest. The document log is independent of the module. Open it with another module to automatically rebuild its derived view in place. Retain the previous bytes to reproduce the previous computation. A new module that cannot process the retained documents raises an error; it does not discard them. Rebuilding starts a new cursor generation even if the outputs happen to match. Deterministic views use explicit inputs and state rather than clocks, randomness, mutable globals, or undeclared external data. Hosts instantiate Wasm modules afresh for operations. Reference inputs must remain reproducible, not merely have a remembered version label. A fold is not automatically mergeable; implement merge only when its laws hold. Stable reads and generation boundaries A snapshot cursor names a database generation, exact module, and committed prefix. Continue a query with both its cursor and after token; new documents do not change that snapshot. Changes carry resulting key states after the chosen cursor, coalesced per key within a batch. A page can split a batch's group updates; zero-emission documents still advance progress. A valid native checkpoint preserves generation and cursors across reopen. Explicit rebuild, a missing or invalid checkpoint requiring reconstruction, or a changed module starts a new generation and expires old cursors. A fresh browser worker also has a new identity. On CursorExpired , obtain a fresh complete snapshot and replace the consumer's entire application state before following its new cursor. The persistent consumer example shows stable snapshot pagination and this replacement branch. Row and document iterators release the engine between pages. No operation lock spans a yield into application code, although a persistent database retains its file-ownership lock until close. History is currently retained; there is no history compaction or reader-expiry policy. The same computation; browser memory The browser worker loads identical Wasm bytes, while JavaScript owns grouping, documents, and history. It does not run the Rust log engine. There is no IndexedDB persistence yet. Reload, close, or a worker deadline discards memory; export resolved records and ingest them into a new worker to restore the view. The browser preview rejects batches above its document, group, history, and byte limits; see component limits . Browser replay() constructs a separate worker-side replay with the original batches and compares keys, states, and results, leaving the current worker's cursors intact. Numerical reproducibility Payloads, keys, states, and results use finite IEEE-754 doubles, matching JavaScript numbers. Python and the native engine reject integer inputs that cannot be represented exactly as a double, rather than rounding them. Encode arbitrary-precision identifiers as strings. Positions and engine sequences remain nonnegative JavaScript-safe integers. JSON nesting is bounded to 64 levels. The same module and canonical key rules give both hosts the same supported computation. Neither adds Python arbitrary-precision arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative: arbitrary merge trees can change rounding. Preserve input order and partition/merge plans when exact agreement matters. Merge compatible states with disjoint coverage, rather than finalized means.

title: Upgrade guide
text: Upgrade guide · 0.4.1 Upgrade to Foldlite DB 0.4.1 Version 0.4.1 ships reproducible in-repo numeric reducers, hardened AssemblyScript portable views, incremental callback checkpoints, and stricter query/get validation while keeping the FOLDLOG2 document log format unchanged. Existing 0.2.0 and 0.3.x logs need no log migration; older 0.1.x logs require the verified copy migration below. The consolidated changelog covers every published release. The 0.2.0 release includes distribution hashes and validation receipts. Upgrade from 0.3.1, 0.3.2, or 0.3.3 Close the database, preserve its log and exact view artifacts, and install foldlitedb==0.4.1 . Open the same log with the same view and compare results. Custom portable Wasm views whose module bytes are unchanged retain their checkpoints, generation, and cursors without replaying checkpointed batches. Bundled portable views ( View.bundled("metrics") , View.bundled("catalogue") ) and the callback document module were rebuilt with hardened JSON/Unicode/decimal parsing, so opening an older bundled database automatically reconstructs its disposable .cache from the unchanged log and starts a fresh cursor generation. Check two tightened Python call signatures before cutover: the optional positional argument on db.query(view_name, ...) and db.rows(view_name, ...) now exclusively names a registered callback view (pass key=... explicitly for exact key selection), and db.get(id=None, *, position=None, source="default") requires either a nonempty string id or a safe integer position rather than both or neither. Native execution continues to use Wasmi 2.0 fuel accounting from 0.3.2+. Rollback to 0.3.x uses the same FOLDLOG2 log after closing the 0.4.1 owner and starting fresh cursors if the disposable cache was rebuilt. Upgrade from 0.2.0 Close the database and preserve a backup of the document log and exact view artifacts, as for any package upgrade. Install foldlitedb==0.4.1 in a separate environment and open the same log with the same view. FOLDLOG2 is unchanged. Unchanged custom Wasm modules restore their compatible checkpoint and reconstruct the query ordering index without rerunning checkpointed Wasm; bundled views automatically rebuild their disposable .cache under the hardened 0.4.1 bundled modules. Start fresh query traversals. 0.2.x after query tokens are rejected explicitly because their ordering and filter binding differ. Saved snapshot/change cursors remain valid when a compatible custom module cache survives; cache reconstruction, bundled module updates, module replacement, or explicit rebuild expires them cleanly so consumers refresh from a new snapshot. Document pagination is unchanged. Check application assumptions about row order and query calls. Numbers sort numerically, strings by Unicode codepoint, arrays by recursive element order, and objects by their ordered members; pass exact key filters via key=... rather than positional arguments. Query ordering changes do not reorder documents, reducer contributions, or change-feed sequences. Use the same selector and inclusive flags on every query page; only limit may change. See the range and prefix reference . Browser deployments must update the complete host and module assets together and obtain new worker cursors. The portable module ABI v1 is unchanged. For rollback to 0.2.0, close the new owner, restore the 0.2.0 module if using bundled views, and use a fresh 0.2.0 query traversal; do not reuse 0.3.x/0.4.x query tokens. The unchanged log format remains readable. Preserve the original backup and computation, and account for any writes made during the upgrade. Before you start The remaining steps upgrade native FOLDLOG1 document logs from 0.1.x to FOLDLOG2 . New 0.2.0 and later databases already use the new format. Browser databases have no native log to migrate; see browser upgrades . Compact external projection caches have a different source of truth; see external projections . Use Python 3.11 or newer. Preserve the exact Wasm module, or Python callback code, versions, references, and other reproducible inputs needed by your view. Migration copies facts and batch boundaries; it does not change your computation or repair already incorrect application data. Plan new snapshot cursors for the migrated database. 1. Stop writers and back up the source Stop producers, background imports, and consumers that hold the database open. Close its owner cleanly before copying files. Copy the original document log to a separate backup location. Keep the view artifacts and reference inputs with that backup. Confirm the copied log exists and has the expected size or checksum. Keep the original filename in place for comparison. Choose a different destination, such as metrics-v2.fold . If the old primary filename uses the newly reserved sidecar namespace, make an independent closed-log copy under a permitted name such as metrics-original.fold and use that copy as the source in steps 3–5. Keep the untouched original as well. This lets the new reader inspect and compare it without bypassing filename protection. The log contains the retained documents. Its .cache sibling is disposable; copying a cache alone is not a backup. Do not delete a live owner's .lock file. Do not use reset=True to upgrade: reset explicitly discards source documents. 2. Install 0.4.1 in a separate environment python -m venv .venv-upgrade . .venv-upgrade/bin/activate python -m pip install --only-binary=:all: foldlitedb==0.4.1 python -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('foldlitedb'))" On Windows Command Prompt, activate with .venv-upgrade\Scripts\activate.bat . Matching wheels need no compiler. For other source-build environments, follow the installation prerequisites . Keep the previous environment available until cutover is complete. 3. Inspect the closed log with its intended view The Python snippets in steps 3–5 run in order in the same session or script, from the directory containing your log. This example uses bundled metrics. For a custom portable view, replace View.bundled("metrics") with your preserved module, for example View("metrics-original.wasm") . For ordinary callback views, pass your preserved callback definition. from pathlib import Path from foldlitedb import Database, View source = Path("metrics.fold") if not source.is_file(): raise FileNotFoundError(source) # Avoid creating an empty database by mistake. view = View.bundled("metrics") with Database(source, view) as original: log = original.stats()["log"] print({"format": log["format"], "read_only": log["read_only"]}) A legacy log reports format: 1 and read_only: True . Reads and export work; new appends fail with migration guidance. If it reports format 2, skip the copy migration: it already uses the current format. Opening may recover an interrupted final frame, which is why the raw closed-log backup comes first. 4. Copy into a new log destination = Path("metrics-v2.fold") if destination.exists(): raise FileExistsError(destination) Database.migrate(source, destination) Both paths must be persistent files in existing parent directories. The destination must not exist and must differ from the source. Primary filenames ending in .cache or .lock , or containing .cache. , are reserved case-insensitively; metrics-v2.fold is suitable. Migration verifies the source, preserves document IDs, sources, positions, order, and original batch boundaries, and leaves source bytes unchanged. It refuses an active owner or an existing destination. If copying fails, it removes its partial destination when possible and reports cleanup failures; inspect any remaining destination before retrying. It does not copy old cursor generations or transplant caches. Ordinary opens reject reserved legacy primary names; explicit migration can copy such an old source into a permitted destination. 5. Compare documents, results, and rebuilt results With writers still stopped, compare resolved documents and view output under the same computation. The verifier streams through bounded pages and excludes database-local cursors and row sequence metadata from the comparison. from itertools import zip_longest def require_equal(left, right, label): missing = object() for number, (a, b) in enumerate(zip_longest(left, right, fillvalue=missing), 1): if a != b: raise RuntimeError(f"{label} differs at entry {number}") def view_values(database): for row in database.rows(): yield row.key, row.state, row.result with Database(source, view) as original, Database(destination, view) as migrated: require_equal(original.documents(), migrated.documents(), "Documents") require_equal(view_values(original), view_values(migrated), "View") migrated.rebuild() require_equal(view_values(original), view_values(migrated), "Rebuilt view") print("Verified", migrated.stats()["documents"], "documents") print("Destination format:", migrated.stats()["log"]["format"]) Expected output names the same document count and destination format 2 . A mismatch stops the upgrade; keep both files and investigate the view artifacts or source data before resuming writes. A cache/checkpoint error reports accelerator failure and does not undo already committed log data. 6. Switch the application and replace cursors Configure the application to use metrics-v2.fold with its verified view and the 0.4.1 environment. Avoid renaming or mixing old sidecars into the new database. Recreate application state from a fresh snapshot. Old cursors belong to the original database generation; portable change-feed consumers must resume from the new snapshot's cursor. Resume one database owner and normal producers. Stable source IDs and positions still support identical retries. Check the application’s expected results and writer health. Keep the original log, backup, and previous environment until the cutover is accepted. Application compatibility checks Area Current behavior and action Callback reads A primary callback supplies query() / rows() . Additional registered callbacks use query(name) ; pass exact key filters via key=... . Snapshot pages are descriptor-bound; historical pages can replay original batches. Callback live feeds and preview Primary callback changes() / preview() explicitly fail. Use fresh query snapshots, or inspect the mapper with a resolved Document . Portable Wasm views retain both operations. Callback code changes Update the view/reducer version or references when behavior or captured inputs change. Ordinary callback caches then reconstruct from documents. Callbacks remain trusted deterministic Python. Metadata sources Source names beginning _ are retained metadata and do not map in either host. If older browser data used such names for observations, resolve that source policy before cutover; copying a log does not rename identities. Numbers Unrepresentable integer inputs are rejected rather than rounded, a rule enforced natively since 0.1.4. Use strings for exact large identifiers. Authoring tools Use the documented Node runtime range to rebuild modules. Installing a matching Python wheel needs no Node runtime. External projection caches materialize_jsonl_view keeps compact cursor/state documents; the external stream is authoritative and its raw history is not retained in that cache. Do not treat that file as a replacement for the external source. Preserve the external stream, generation identity, callback code, and references. Close the old cache owner, select a fresh permitted cache filename, and run the helper against the verified external source with 0.4.1. This regenerates state and consumed progress together. Copy migration is available if retaining a legacy cache is necessary, but it does not turn compact metadata into a source archive. A changed descriptor or source generation must reconstruct from the external source; historical external snapshots are unavailable. Browser upgrades Export resolved documents before reloading or closing the old worker. Deploy the complete new portable_assets directory, including modules, manifests, and client/worker/host/error files; do not mix old hosts with new manifests or Wasm. Start a new worker, ingest the exported records with their original IDs, sources, positions, and order, and compare keys, states, and results. Obtain new cursors. Browser state remains in memory and has no native log migration step. Rollback Before the new log accepts writes, rollback means returning the application to the untouched original log and its matching previous environment/view. Older binaries do not understand FOLDLOG2; an in-place downgrade is unsupported. After new writes, the original file no longer contains all accepted observations. Preserve both logs and plan replay/reconciliation of the new observations from your authoritative source before switching back. Simply pointing at the old filename would omit those writes. Never discard the converted log as part of an unverified rollback. If a step fails Message or symptom Next step Legacy log is read-only Complete copy migration and configure the new filename. Already open or cannot be locked Stop and close every owner. Do not remove the ownership lock to bypass it. Destination exists Choose a fresh filename or inspect the existing migrated copy. Do not reset or overwrite it to retry. Migration source has an incomplete tail Keep the raw backup. FOLDLOG1 copy migration automatically skips an incomplete torn final frame while leaving the source untouched; for a FOLDLOG2 source with an interrupted final frame, open and close a working copy normally first to recover the tail, then retry migration. Complete-frame corruption must fail; do not edit or remove frames to force acceptance. Unsupported or corrupt header Confirm that this is a Foldlite native document log and that the backup is intact. Copy migration does not convert another database's format. Checkpoint or close fails Keep the document log. Fix the reported cache-path, disk-space, or size issue; a failed accelerator save does not roll back durable appends. See documents and caches .
